title: QPanda: high-performance quantum computing framework for multiple application scenarios
abstract_summary: This preprint presents QPanda, a high-performance, multi-scenario quantum programming framework designed to support applications in quantum finance, chemistry, fluid mechanics, and machine learning. QPanda provides multiple simulation backends (full/partial/single-amplitude, MPS, and noise-inclusive), CPU/GPU/OpenMP optimizations, circuit fusion and compilation tools (including mapping to QPU topologies and OriginIR), and a quantum–supercomputer hybrid backend; experiments report improved simulation performance and higher fidelity for compiled circuits on QPUs.
methodology_description: The paper presents the design, implementation and evaluation methodology for QPanda, a multi-scenario quantum programming framework. Method workstreams include: (1) framework design and implementation of multiple simulation backends (full-amplitude, partial-amplitude, single-amplitude, matrix-product-state/tensor-network and an adjustable-noise simulator), CPU and GPU compute backends, OpenMP multithreading, GPU kernels and memory-hierarchy-aware allocation, and circuit-level optimizations (gate fusion, merging, identity removal and synthesis into target basis gates); (2) a compilation pipeline to decompose multi-control gates, translate to chip basis gates, map virtual to physical qubits with an opt-BMT mapping algorithm (OBMT_mapping), and emit OriginIR for OriginQ QPUs; (3) a quantum-supercomputer fusion design for splitting/partitioning large circuits and running subcircuits on classical HPC nodes; (4) tooling (VQC/variational circuits, Hamiltonian and operator utilities, QIf/QWhile, visualization, conversion to QASM/Quil/OriginIR); and (5) empirical benchmarking and experiments: microbenchmarks of per-gate simulation time, end-to-end random-circuit simulation timing under several configurations (single-thread, multi-thread, with/without circuit optimization and OpenMP, CPU vs GPU), and comparative benchmarks versus other simulators (Qulacs, Qiskit, ProjectQ, Cirq). Additional experiments include mapping and optimization effects on QAOA circuits across different chip topologies (grid and cycle) measuring circuit depth and CNOT counts, and demonstration of noise modeling using Kraus operators and configurable readout/rotation errors. Performance metrics focus on execution time (seconds, relative time) and compiled-circuit metrics (depth, CNOT count); fidelity is discussed qualitatively for compiled circuits on QPUs.
experimental_setup: Benchmarks run on a CentOS system with Intel Core i9-9900K CPU (3.60 GHz) and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU (24 GB). Software toolchain: GCC 7.3.0, Python 3.9.0. Simulation backends exercised include CPUQVM (full amplitude), PartialAmpQVM, SingleAmpQVM, MPSQVM, NoiseQVM, and GPUQVM. Benchmarks used random two-layer circuits (rotation layer of RX/RY/RZ followed by CNOT layer with target i and control (i+1) mod n). Tests varied qubit counts (e.g. 5–25 qubits), compared single-thread and multi-thread execution, and toggled circuit optimization (fusion) and OpenMP. Comparative experiments measured total circuit build/compile/execute time across libraries. Additional experiments measured mapping/optimization impact on QAOA circuits across grid and cycle topologies by recording circuit depth and CNOT counts pre- and post-optimization.

experiment_process.overview: Construct random benchmark circuits and specific algorithm circuits (e.g., QAOA). For random benchmarks the circuit pattern is a rotation layer (RX, RY, RZ on each qubit) followed by a CNOT layer with specified control-target pairing. For QAOA mapping experiments, prepare QAOA circuits of varying qubit sizes mapped onto different chip topologies (grid, cycle).

results_summary: The paper introduces QPanda, a quantum programming framework emphasizing multi-scenario support (finance, chemistry, ML, CFD) and high-performance simulation. It implements multiple simulators (state-vector, partial amplitude, single-amplitude / path-sum, tensor-network / MPS), an adjustable Kraus-based noise backend, and compilation/optimization passes (gate decomposition, basis translation, gate fusion/merging, and topology-aware mapping). Empirical benchmarks reported by the authors indicate that QPanda achieves better CPU single-thread and multi-thread simulation runtimes than several contemporary frameworks (Qulacs, Qiskit, ProjectQ, Cirq) in their tests, and demonstrates strong GPU performance. Compilation and mapping reduce circuit depth and CNOT counts for sample QAOA circuits, and the authors report that compiled circuits run with high fidelity on their QPU target. Many broader claims about enabling domain applications and large-scale quantum-supercomputer fusion are prospective and not demonstrated at application scale in this paper.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper focuses on a programming framework, simulation performance, and compilation/optimization workflows; it does not claim nor demonstrate a domain-level quantum advantage (speedup or solution quality beyond classical methods) for financial or other application workloads.
limitations: NISQ devices are limited in qubit count, have small quantum volume and significant noise, constraining direct execution of many algorithms.
Classical simulation of quantum circuits scales exponentially with qubit number (memory and time), so full-amplitude simulation is memory-limited.
Feynman-path (single-amplitude) simulation scales exponentially with gate count, making it impractical for deep circuits.
Circuit partitioning (splitting) to handle large circuits incurs considerable cost and complexity.
QPU topology, coherence times and gate errors require mapping and compilation steps; these constraints limit what can be executed on real hardware and affect fidelity.
Noise on real QPUs is complex and time-varying; the framework provides adjustable, parametrized noise models but real-device noise characterization and mitigation remain challenging.

OpenMP multi-threading introduces overhead and can increase memory use; for some intermediate circuit sizes (authors cite ~11–12 qubits) adaptive multithreading or fusion can decrease rather than increase performance.
Quantum circuit optimization/fusion can improve simulation and execution but may have diminishing returns or interactions with parallelization choices that need careful tuning.
The paper does not demonstrate large-scale QPU experiments; fidelity claims are qualitative/limited in detail in the manuscript.

open_questions: Which specific quantum algorithms will bring practical advantage for the targeted industrial application domains (finance, chemistry, fluid mechanics, etc.) on NISQ-era devices?
How effective are the presented compilation, mapping and optimization techniques at improving end-to-end fidelity on real, noisy QPUs in varied topologies and noise landscapes?
What are the trade-offs between circuit fusion/optimization and parallelization strategies (OpenMP/GPU) across different circuit sizes and structures?
How well do the adjustable Kraus-noise models and ML-trained noise approximations capture real device noise for reliable error-mitigation and robustness studies?
How effective and scalable is the quantum-supercomputer fusion approach in practice for large, application-level circuits, considering partitioning overheads and hybrid execution coordination?
To what extent can partial-amplitude, single-amplitude and tensor-network (MPS) simulators cover the algorithmic workloads of interest (e.g., QAOA, VQE) before hitting resource bottlenecks?
How portable are QPanda-compiled programs (OriginIR) to other hardware platforms and how much effort is needed to integrate with other ecosystems (e.g., Cirq, PennyLane, IBM, Rigetti)?
What are the best practices for selecting among the multiple simulation backends (full amplitude, partial amplitude, single amplitude, MPS, noisy) for a given research or application scenario?
How do circuit-splitting and subcircuit selection heuristics impact final result fidelity and total resource consumption when offloading parts to classical or quantum hardware?

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — QPanda implements a quantum–supercomputer hybrid backend to partition large circuits and run subcircuits on classical HPC nodes, enabling larger end-to-end workflows than pure-QPU pipelines.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The framework targets NISQ-era workloads with variational circuits (VQC/QAOA), noise-inclusive simulation (Kraus models, readout/rotation errors), and compilation/mapping tuned for current chip topologies.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Provides a full compilation pipeline (gate decomposition, OBMT_mapping, basis synthesis, OriginIR emission) to bridge high-level algorithms to QPU backends, reducing manual mapping effort.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Circuit-level optimizations (fusion, gate merging, identity removal) and topology-aware mapping materially reduce circuit depth and CNOT counts in QAOA mapping experiments, which is important for NISQ fidelity.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Multiple simulation backends (full/partial/single-amplitude, MPS/tensor-network, noise-inclusive) and CPU/GPU/OpenMP optimizations enable benchmarking and debugging of algorithms up to ~25 qubits on classical hardware.

#idea:hybrid-approach — GPU kernels and memory-aware allocation plus multithreading show several-fold execution-time improvements versus unoptimized runs and competitive performance against other simulators (Qulacs, Qiskit, ProjectQ, Cirq).
#limitation:simulation-only — All experimental results are from classical simulators (CPU/GPU/MPS/NoiseQVM); no real QPU execution or quantitative fidelity measurements on hardware are reported.
#limitation:qubit-count — Benchmarks are demonstrated up to ~25 qubits (simulation limits), so scalability to production-scale quantum workloads is not empirically shown.

#limitation:noise — Noise modeling is supported for experimentation, but real-hardware noise behavior and mitigation strategies are not validated empirically; fidelity claims for compiled circuits on QPUs are qualitative.
